abstract: A book thatbecame the basis for modern communication theory, by a scientist considered one of the founders of the field of artifical intelligence. Some predict that Norbert Wiener will be remembered for his Extrapolation long after Cybernetics is forgotten. Indeed, few computer science students would know today what cybernetics is all about, while every communication student knows what Wiener's filter is. The original work was circulated as a classified memorandum in 1942, because it was connected with sensitive wartime efforts to improve radar communication. This book became the basis for modern communication theory, by a scientist considered one of the founders of the field of artifical intelligence. Combining ideas from statistics and time-series analysis, Wiener used Gauss's method of shaping the characteristic of a detector to allow for the maximal recognition of signals in the presence of noise. This method came to be known as the "Wiener filter."

narrative:
Short impact summary

Extrapolation, Interpolation, and Smoothing of Stationary Time Series (1949), published by The MIT Press, has been cited 4,839 times — enough that OpenAlex puts it in the top 1% of works in its field and year.

Full narrative

Extrapolation, Interpolation, and Smoothing of Stationary Time Series by Norbert Wiener was published by The MIT Press in 1949. It is part of the The MIT Press series. Conceptually, the work connects to Wiener filter, Extrapolation, Gauss, Cybernetics and Communication theory.

OpenAlex records 4,839 citations. That places it in the top 1% of works in its field and year of publication. Citations peaked in 2018 with 204 citing works. Notable citing venues include Cambridge University Press eBooks, arXiv (Cornell University) and IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. Of 1,654 citation statements scite has classified, 10 support its claims, 1,611 mention it in passing, and none contradict it. The citing works include 2,894 journal articles, 585 book chapters and 179 dissertations. They come from 40 countries, led by the United States, the United Kingdom and Germany.

Open Library reports a combined count of 2 reading logs and catalog editions.
